questions.question: In an R1CS instance, what does it mean for a witness w to satisfy a constraint (A, B, C)?
options: A(w) + B(w) = C(w) (mod p)
A(w) · B(w) = C(w) (mod p)
A and B are constant matrices; only C depends on w
C(w) must be invertible (non-zero) (mod p)
questions.explanation: Each constraint enforces one field equation: the product of two linear combinations equals a third, modulo p.

questions.question: Why do many R1CS systems reserve w[0] = 1?
options: To make every witness unique by definition
To represent constants inside linear combinations
To prevent negative numbers from appearing
To ensure all constraints are linear
questions.explanation: With w[0]=1, any constant term can be expressed as a coefficient on wire 0 in A, B, or C.

questions.question: Which of the following correctly encodes an addition gate s = x + y as an R1CS constraint?
options: x · y = s
questions.explanation: Addition is linear, so you can set B=1 and enforce A(w)·1 = C(w).

questions.question: In the lesson circuit out = (x+y)(x-y), why do we introduce intermediate wires s and d?
options: R1CS forbids multiplication, so we avoid it
R1CS requires every non-linear expression to be named by a wire
Intermediate wires are only for optimization and can always be skipped
To make the witness smaller
questions.explanation: R1CS constraints talk about linear combinations of wires; to reuse a subexpression like (x+y), you allocate a wire for it.

questions.question: Suppose a constraint fails. Which triple is the most useful local debug data for that constraint?
options: The list of all constraints in the system
The prover’s source code for the circuit
A(w), B(w), and C(w) values for the failing constraint
Only whether the verifier accepted or rejected
questions.explanation: Computing A(w), B(w), C(w) shows exactly what equation was expected and which side is wrong.

questions.question: What is the key difference between “R1CS constraints satisfied” and “a zero-knowledge proof verified”?
options: Constraint satisfaction already implies zero-knowledge
Constraint satisfaction is a statement; proof verification is evidence of that statement without revealing the witness
Proof verification only checks addition constraints, not multiplication constraints
Zero-knowledge proof verification does not depend on the field modulus
questions.explanation: R1CS satisfiability defines the relation; a proof system provides a (usually succinct) protocol to convince a verifier of satisfiability.

questions.question: Attack-themed: if a circuit intends to prove an integer relation (e.g., “v is in [0, 2^32)”) but you only enforce equations in F_p, what can go wrong?
options: Nothing: field equations always preserve integer meaning
The prover can use wrap-around values (mod p) that satisfy equations but violate the intended integer range
The verifier can recover the witness from the equations
The constraint system becomes non-deterministic
questions.explanation: Field arithmetic is modulo p, so without explicit range constraints, a value can be interpreted as a different integer representative and still satisfy equations.

questions.question: If a prover and verifier disagree on the indexing/order of witness wires, what is the most likely outcome?
options: Constraints still verify because R1CS is commutative
Some constraints may accidentally pass, but the system is not well-defined and verification will generally fail
The witness becomes public automatically
Only the first constraint can fail; the rest are unaffected
questions.explanation: Linear combinations refer to wire indices; inconsistent ordering means you’re checking different equations than you think you are.
